We investigate whether increasing the number of mutually agreeing poisoned documents affects a model's ability to detect misinformation. We evaluate 200 randomly selected questions from SciFact (random seed 38), comparing contexts with one poisoned and six healthy documents against contexts with six mutually agreeing poisoned documents and one healthy document. Our results provide initial evidence of conformity bias in RAG-based misinformation detection: Gemma-3-12b is substantially less likely to detect poisoned claims when they dominate the retrieved evidence.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:76a7c11f2545f3f8f1417e82969b14825103c6058d7d730c1e4dda44ebd82e8e","span_id":"span-a723f9817c67d15fe33feda2cb02ed38","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.41012:v1:metadata-f20dbad8ce03c4ef","work_id":"arxiv:2610.41012"},"u80078b460a7fe1d0f0ca":{"end":1488,"material_id":"mat-712c4b3179b5eae15fbed75fbbf4711f","page":null,"parser_revision":"workspace-plain-text-v1","quote":"To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:7b571028378bb667ba7070192a7022eb9bd0dfca34a047f85897de249eebdb1d","span_id":"span-abaa8d7a8435a0316a96ac41bd90d84d","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.40700:v1:metadata-c05b44ce3bd6d5f0","work_id":"arxiv:2610.40700"}}}}

We introduce Certified Anchor-Based Adaptation (CABA), a candidate-agnostic post-update gate that reserves historical observations from candidate optimization, compares old and candidate policies on frozen representations, and selects the largest tested interpolation coefficient whose worst-anchor forward KL divergence remains within budget. The finite check requires neither action labels nor complete trajectories. We develop a theory-led certification framework that separates measured anchor retention from conditional off-anchor guarantees. Under explicit representation-coverage and Lipschitz assumptions, an accepted update satisfies a uniform behavioral-divergence bound on protected support. The analysis gives regularity bounds for affine softmax heads, probabilistic coverage and compression guarantees, interpolation monotonicity conditions, grid-resolution bounds, and trajectory-level and sequential-composition guarantees. In a controlled UCI Human Activity Recognition study used as a non-stationary sensor-policy proxy, CABA reduces mean forgetting from 1.01 percent for unconstrained adaptation to 0.00 percent at budget epsilon = 0.05, while reducing final average accuracy from 93.04 percent to 88.48 percent. The experiment illustrates a retention-plasticity trade-off and does not establish foundation-model or robotic performance.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:f4e1962813f021fb1d1b0862b88a67b02e88d3f7b80c8c332c6c60a011260a6b","span_id":"span-a8ceea84e4c90c2a0d0f04f7f52bf2ee","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.40740:v1:metadata-b471d2e5f0142ad7","work_id":"arxiv:2610.40740"},"ud74690491a54da4f33b6":{"end":1597,"material_id":"mat-37637e07527abf0d35a62bf375e4ad57","page":null,"parser_revision":"workspace-plain-text-v1","quote":"This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.","scope":"abstract","source_hash":"sha256:57d828d72e965955c14487b74cfd406d58aeab909942be50c97cafac89d3ccae","span_id":"span-61a1d0725d68ccf9dad4480109110d91","start":0,"version_id":"arxiv:2610.41552:v1:metadata-1c364e8ae805a931","work_id":"arxiv:2610.41552"}}}}
